questions.q: A menu is printed from flat category rows by calling childrenOf(id), which scans all n rows, once for the top level and once for every category. How does the work grow?
questions.explain: Printing is O(n), but finding children is not: each of the n + 1 calls loops over all n rows, so the comparisons are (n + 1) × n. Building a map from id to node first makes the whole walk O(n).
options: O(n), because each category is printed once
O(log n), because the menu is nested
O(n²), because about n + 1 calls each scan n rows
O(2ⁿ), because the recursion branches

questions.q: Which structure is not a tree?
questions.explain: A tree needs one root, exactly one parent for every other node, and no loops. A and B form a loop: following parents from A never reaches the root. A single node, a wide tree and a chain are all valid trees.
options: One node with no children
A root with 50 children that are all leaves
Categories A and B where A's parent is B and B's parent is A, under a root
A chain where every node has exactly one child except the last

questions.q: A category tree has 250 nodes. How many parent-child edges does it have?
questions.explain: Every node except the root has exactly one edge up to its parent, so a tree with n nodes always has n − 1 edges, whatever its shape.
options: It depends on the shape

questions.q: In the tree All → Electronics → Phones → Android, what are the depth of Phones and the height of Electronics? (Assume Android is a leaf and Electronics has no other deeper branch.)
questions.explain: Depth counts edges down from the root: All → Electronics → Phones is 2 edges. Height counts edges from a node down to its deepest leaf: Electronics → Phones → Android is 2 edges.
options: depth 3, height 1
depth 2, height 2
depth 1, height 3
depth 2, height 3

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A leaf has no children, so tallest stays −1 and the height is 0. shop reaches leaf through two edges, so its height is 2. Counting nodes instead of edges would give 1 and 3.

questions.q: Why does buildTree use a Map from id to node?
questions.explain: With the map, each row finds its parent node in O(1) on average, so two passes over n rows cost O(n). A Map does not sort keys, and set silently overwrites duplicates: you have to detect those yourself.
options: Because a Map keeps the rows sorted by id
So attaching each row to its parent is an O(1) lookup instead of a scan, making the whole build O(n)
Because objects cannot hold arrays of children
So that duplicate ids are detected automatically

questions.q: buildTree first creates a node for every row, and only then links children to parents in a second loop. What would go wrong if it did both in one loop?
questions.explain: Database rows arrive in any order. If a child row comes before its parent, a single loop tries to attach it to a node that does not exist yet. Creating all nodes first removes that ordering assumption.
options: Nothing; one loop is always equivalent
A row whose parent appears later in the array would find no parent node yet
The tree would come out in reverse order
It would become O(n²)

questions.q: A category's parent was deleted. What does this print?
questions.explain: byId.get(42) is undefined, and reading .children of undefined throws a TypeError. One bad row crashes the whole build unless you check for a missing parent.
options: TypeError
built
RangeError
ReferenceError

questions.q: Two categories are each other's parent. How does the safe builder in the lesson notice?
questions.explain: Building does not crash: the two nodes simply hang off each other. A walk from the root never reaches them, so total nodes − reached nodes is the number stuck in loops. That check is O(n) and cannot loop forever itself.
options: It follows parents upward from every node until it finds a repeat
It counts the nodes reachable from the root by following children; nodes in a loop are never reached
JavaScript throws a RangeError while building
The Map refuses to store a node twice

questions.q: The breadcrumb function walks up through parentId and throws if the path grows longer than the number of categories. Why is that a correct loop check?
questions.explain: A path from a node up to the root has distinct nodes, so its length is at most the number of categories. Anything longer revisits a node: the data contains a loop. The check stops an infinite loop with a clear error.
options: Because breadcrumbs are never longer than 3 items
A real path visits each category at most once, so a longer path must repeat a category, which means a loop
Because JavaScript arrays cannot hold more items than the Map
It is not correct; it rejects valid deep trees

questions.q: You need the total size of every folder in a directory tree. Which traversal fits?
questions.explain: A folder's size is the sum of its children's sizes, so the children must be finished first. Post-order does exactly that; it is what du does.
options: Pre-order
Post-order
Level order
Any order, because addition is commutative

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The name is pushed after the children are walked: post-order. logo finishes first, then its parent images, then cart, and the root shop comes last.
options: logo images cart shop
shop images logo cart
shop images cart logo
cart logo images shop

questions.q: What does this level-order walk print?
questions.explain: A queue hands out nodes in the order they were added: first the root, then both depth-1 nodes, then the depth-2 nodes. The depth-first (pre-order) answer would be All, Electronics, Phones, Fashion, Shoes.
options: All, Electronics, Fashion, Phones, Shoes
All, Electronics, Phones, Fashion, Shoes
Phones, Electronics, Shoes, Fashion, All
All, Fashion, Shoes, Electronics, Phones

questions.q: Why did the lesson's level-order walk use an array with a head index instead of queue.shift()?
questions.explain: shift() takes the first element correctly, but it has to reindex all the others. Advancing a head index is O(1). (The index approach actually keeps the used entries in memory; a proper queue from the stacks-and-queues lesson avoids that too.)
options: shift() removes from the wrong end
shift() moves every remaining element down, so each call is O(n) and the walk can become O(n²)
shift() does not exist on arrays
The head index uses less memory

questions.q: An iterative walk takes the next node from a collection of waiting nodes. What single change turns a depth-first walk into a breadth-first one?
questions.explain: With a stack (newest first) the walk dives down one branch: depth-first. With a queue (oldest first) it finishes each level before the next: breadth-first. Everything else in the loop stays the same.
options: Visiting children before parents
Taking the oldest waiting node (a queue) instead of the newest (a stack)
Using recursion instead of a loop
Sorting the children first

questions.q: This iterative walk pushes children in their normal order. What does it print?
questions.explain: The stack is last in, first out. After A, B and then C are pushed, so C is popped first. The result is a depth-first walk, but right to left. Push children in reverse to get the usual pre-order ABDC.
options: ACBD
ABDC
ABCD
DBCA

questions.q: A recursive traversal of a tree with n nodes and height h takes O(n) time. How much extra memory does the call stack need?
questions.explain: At any moment the stack holds one frame per node on the path from the root to the current node, so at most h + 1 frames. For a balanced tree that is O(log n); for a chain it is O(n).
options: O(h)
O(n²)
O(log n) always

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The chain is 200,000 levels deep, so the recursion needs 200,000 stack frames. The engine allows far fewer and throws RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded. An explicit stack in an array handles it easily.
options: RangeError
TypeError

questions.q: Your API accepts nested JSON comments from users and walks them recursively. What is the production risk, and the fix?
questions.explain: Input you do not control can be as deep as the attacker likes. A recursive walk uses one frame per level and throws a RangeError. Rejecting inputs deeper than a sensible limit, or walking with an array as a stack, removes the risk.
options: No risk; JSON cannot be nested deeply
A deeply nested payload can overflow the call stack and crash the request; cap the depth or use an explicit stack
Recursion is slower, so switch to a for loop over the top level only
The risk is memory; use a WeakMap

questions.q: A perfect binary tree has height 9. How many nodes does it have?
questions.explain: A perfect tree of height h has 2h+1 − 1 nodes: 210 − 1 = 1023. Turned around, the height of a balanced tree grows with log₂ n.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Post-order lists both operands before their operator. The + subtree comes first (2000 500 +), then the right leaf 2, then the root *. That is the order a calculator evaluates it: (2000 + 500) × 2.

questions.q: What exactly does the BST invariant require?
questions.explain: The rule is about whole subtrees, not just direct children. A key two levels down that sits on the wrong side of its grandparent breaks the tree even if every parent-child pair looks right.
options: Each node's left child is smaller and its right child is larger
For every node, all keys in its left subtree are smaller and all keys in its right subtree are larger
Keys increase from the root down to the leaves
The tree is balanced

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: 60 is a correct right child of 30, so the child-only check passes. But 60 is in the left subtree of 50, where every key must be below 50. The range check carries that upper bound down and rejects it.
options: true false
false false
true true
false true

questions.q: Keys are inserted into an empty BST in this order. How many comparisons does get(45) make?
questions.explain: 45 was inserted below 40: 50 → left to 30 → right to 40 → right to 45. The search follows the same path: 50, 30, 40, 45 is 4 comparisons. A search always walks one root-to-node path, so it costs O(h).

questions.q: Why does an in-order walk of a valid BST produce the keys in ascending order?
questions.explain: In-order is left, node, right. The BST invariant says the left subtree holds exactly the smaller keys and the right subtree the larger ones, so by induction every subtree comes out sorted, whatever the insert order or shape.
options: Because keys are inserted in ascending order
It visits everything smaller (the left subtree) before a node and everything larger (the right subtree) after it, at every node
Because the walk sorts the keys as it goes
It only works for balanced trees

questions.q: You delete a BST node that has two children. Which key can replace it without breaking the invariant?
questions.explain: The successor is larger than everything on the left (it came from the right) and smaller than everything else on the right (it is the smallest there). Then you delete the successor from the right subtree; it has no left child, so that is an easy case. The largest key on the left works too.
options: Its left child's key
The root's key
The smallest key in its right subtree (its in-order successor)
The largest key in its right subtree

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: 50 has two children, so its successor, the smallest key on the right (60), is copied into the root. Then 60 is removed from the right subtree; it had one child, 65, which moves up into its place as 70's left child.

questions.q: Why does the lesson's #remove(node, key) return a node, with callers writing node.left = this.#remove(node.left, key)?
questions.explain: Deleting a leaf returns null, deleting a node with one child returns that child. Returning the new subtree root and assigning it in the parent handles all cases, including the root, without tracking parent pointers.
options: To make the method chainable
The subtree's root may change (to a child or to null), and the parent must store the new one; this handles deleting the tree's root too
Because private methods must return a value
To count comparisons

questions.q: Order ids 1, 2, 3, …, 10,000 are inserted into a plain BST in that order. What happens?
questions.explain: A plain BST does nothing to keep its shape. Sorted input builds a chain leaning right, which is a linked list with extra steps: find, insert and delete all become O(n), and building it costs O(n²). Ids and timestamps are very often sorted, so this is a real risk.
options: The tree balances itself, height about 13
Each key becomes the right child of the previous one: height 9,999, and lookups are O(n)
The inserts fail after the first 1,024 keys
The tree has height about 20 because the ids are unique

questions.q: What does it mean for a family of trees to be balanced?
questions.explain: Balance is about height: AVL and red-black trees use different local rules, but both guarantee height O(log n), so every operation stays O(log n). Equal leaf depth is the much stricter "perfect" shape.
options: Every node has exactly two children
The left and right subtrees of the root have the same size
The height stays O(log n) no matter the order of inserts and deletes
All leaves are at the same depth

questions.q: Why do databases use B-trees (nodes with many keys and many children) for indexes instead of binary search trees?
questions.explain: Reading a page from disk costs far more than comparing keys in memory. With hundreds of keys per node, a B-tree over millions of rows is only three or four levels deep, so a lookup touches three or four pages.
options: B-trees do not need their keys to be sorted
Each node fills a disk page, so the tree is very short and a lookup reads only a few pages
Binary trees cannot store strings
B-trees use less CPU per comparison

questions.q: An in-memory service needs only "get the order with this id" and "add an order". Which structure is the best default in JavaScript?
questions.explain: Without ordered queries, a hash map gives O(1) average lookup and insert, and it is built in. A BST earns its place only when you also need keys in order, ranges or min/max with frequent changes.
options: A hand-written binary search tree
A Map
A sorted array with binary search
A linked list

questions.q: Which requirement most clearly calls for a balanced search tree rather than a Map or a sorted array?
questions.explain: A Map cannot answer range queries without scanning everything, and a sorted array pays O(n) per insert or delete. A balanced tree does inserts, deletes and range queries in O(log n + k).
options: Lookups by exact id, millions of times per second
A list of 20 settings that never changes
Frequent inserts and deletes, plus queries such as "all bookings between 10:00 and 12:00"
Counting how often each word appears

questions.q: The lesson tests the BST by running 2,000 random operations against a sorted array. What is the array's role?
questions.explain: Model-based testing compares a clever implementation with a slow but obviously correct one on many operations. Checking the invariant and the contents after each step finds bugs that only appear after a specific sequence, and the fixed seed makes failures replayable.
options: It makes the BST faster
It is a simple, obviously correct reference model; after every operation the BST must agree with it
It stores the random seed
It checks the tree is balanced

questions.q: Finish countLeaves(node): return how many nodes in the tree have no children. It should print 4.
questions.explain: The base case is a leaf, which counts as 1. Any other node's answer is the sum of its children's answers. Every node is visited once: O(n).

questions.q: Finish buildTree(rows) in O(n): return a root { name: "All", children: [] } with every row attached under its parent (parentId: null means directly under the root). The program prints the menu.
questions.explain: Create every node first, keyed by id in a Map, then link each one to its parent with an O(1) lookup. Android comes before Phones in the rows, which is why the two passes matter.

questions.q: Finish widestLevel(root): walk the tree level by level with a queue and return the largest number of nodes found at any single depth. It should print 3.
questions.explain: Carry each node's depth into the queue and count nodes per depth. Depth 2 holds Phones, Laptops and Shoes. The width is also the most memory a level-order walk ever needs for its queue.

questions.q: Finish insert(root, key) for a BST (return the root; ignore duplicates) and inorder(node, out). The program should print the keys sorted: 2005 3020 4100 5040 7011.
questions.explain: Insert walks left for smaller keys and right for larger ones until it finds an empty slot, and returns the (possibly new) root so the parent can store it. The duplicate 3020 matches neither branch and is ignored. In-order (left, node, right) then yields the keys sorted.

questions.q: Finish isValidBST(node, low, high) so it checks the full BST invariant (not only direct children). It should print true false.
questions.explain: Going left lowers the upper bound to the current key; going right raises the lower bound. Every node must fit between all the limits its ancestors set, which is exactly the invariant. It visits each node once: O(n).

questions.q: A support page shows the category a customer can reach in the fewest clicks that has no subcategories. Finish nearestLeaf(root): return the name of the leaf with the smallest depth (use level order, so you can stop at the first leaf). It should print Laptops.
questions.explain: Level order meets nodes in order of depth, so the first leaf it finds is a shallowest one and it can stop there. A depth-first walk would reach Android first and would have to explore the whole tree to be sure.

questions.q: Finish kthSmallest(root, k) for a BST: return the k-th smallest key (k = 1 is the smallest) using an in-order walk that stops as soon as it has the answer. It should print 4100 7011.
questions.explain: In-order visits keys in ascending order, so the k-th visited key is the answer. Stopping early makes it O(h + k) instead of O(n). A recursive walk with a counter works too.

questions.q: The category data contains a loop. What does this print?
questions.explain: Category 1 reaches the top at once. Category 2 goes Gadgets → Accessories → Gadgets → … forever; after 4 names the path is longer than the 3 categories that exist, so the guard throws. The function is a loop, not recursion, so without the guard it would hang rather than overflow the stack.
options:
Electronics
loop above category 2

Electronics
Accessories > Gadgets

Electronics
RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded
Electronics

questions.q: How many nodes does this range query visit?
questions.explain: It visits 40, 60, 50 and 70. At 40 the whole left subtree (20, 10, 30) is skipped, because nothing there can be 45 or more. At 60 it goes left to 50 (a match) and, since 60 < 65, also right to 70, which is out of range and has no children. The cost is O(h + k): the pruning is what keeps it below O(n).

questions.q: Delivery bands are stored in a BST keyed by the starting weight in kg. Finish floor(root, weight): return the node with the largest key that is less than or equal to weight, in one walk down the tree. It should print 2800 4500 12000.
questions.explain: A key that is small enough is a candidate: remember it and go right to look for a larger one that still fits. A key that is too big sends you left. One path from the root: O(h).
